profile.reading:
Flexential's own Denver-market overview page, re-fetched directly this session at the stored downtown-data-center URL, still renders only a four-facility Denver metro summary (Aurora, Centennial, Englewood, and Parker) with no fifth "Downtown Denver" facility separately named or addressed, consistent with an earlier session's finding. An uncorroborated former ViaWest downtown Denver address (1500 Champa Street) surfaced in prior research but could not be confirmed against any current Flexential source, so it is not asserted here. This is a deliberate, documented gap rather than a research shortfall: no address, square footage, or MW figure is asserted for this specific registry row. This building sits in the Denver-Aurora corridor local reporting has dubbed "Data Center Row," which also includes a major QTS facility under construction in Aurora. Xcel Energy, the region's dominant utility, said in 2025 it was seeking to invest $22 billion to add 12 to 14 gigawatts of new generation and transmission capacity by 2040, driven substantially by data center demand; the utility reported pending data center applications for 5.8 gigawatts of electricity, nearly matching its entire existing 6.2-gigawatt Colorado generating capacity, per Colorado Sun's reporting. Regulators have voiced skepticism about the reliability of these demand forecasts, warning ratepayers could face stranded-asset costs if projected demand fails to materialize.

The QTS facility anchoring the Aurora side of "Data Center Row" is planned at 177 megawatts of capacity on 80 acres at the I-70/C-470 interchange, positioned to become Xcel Energy's largest industrial customer in Colorado, on par with Evraz Rocky Mountain Steel in Pueblo, a marked shift from Xcel's historical major customers in mining and manufacturing, per Colorado Sun's 2023 reporting. That single campus is expected to require 160 megawatts of peak load delivered via a $28 million high-voltage transmission line, ramping up over roughly a decade, with Xcel anticipating similar-scale loads from other emerging data center customers in the region. For QTS, electricity was reported to represent about 40% of operating costs, underscoring why competitive utility rates were central to the Aurora site decision, a dynamic shared broadly across Colorado's Front Range data center corridor.

reading.body:
Flexential Denver - Downtown claims 759,000 square feet of technical space but publishes no power capacity, making it impossible to assess its role in Colorado's AI infrastructure.

The operator's website lists four other Denver metro facilities by name and location, Aurora, Centennial, Englewood, and Parker, but does not identify this Downtown property as a distinct operating site. Flexential's own marketing materials do not confirm the facility exists as a separate asset or describe its current status. This gap between claimed capacity and public verification complicates any assessment of whether the space is built out, powered, and running compute workloads.

Colorado has 17 mapped data center facilities on record. Only three publish power capacity figures. Those three disclose 26.35 MW total. The state's actual power footprint for AI workloads is almost certainly higher than published figures show, since most operators do not release capacity data. Without disclosure from Flexential, this facility cannot be ranked among the state's capacity constraints or integrated into grid planning models.

Technical square footage alone tells you nothing about power draw, power source, or occupancy. The binding constraint on AI scaling is power, not floor space. A facility this size could draw anywhere from negligible capacity to hundreds of megawatts depending on build-out and utilization. Until the operator publishes a power figure, this asset is invisible to anyone planning Colorado's AI-driven grid expansion.
